Weather systems operate through the interaction of pressure differentials, moisture content, and thermal gradients. A low-pressure system (often designated "L" on synoptic charts) draws surrounding air inward and upward, producing condensation and, consequently, precipitation. The process is governed by well-understood thermodynamic principles, though the precise timing of rainfall events remains computationally intensive to predict.

Temperature inversions deserve particular attention. When a layer of warm air overlies cooler air (the inverse of the typical lapse rate), vertical mixing is suppressed. This condition frequently produces fog in coastal regions and traps pollutants in urban valleys. The phenomenon is measurable, reproducible, and significant in both meteorological and public health contexts.

It is worth noting that climate (the statistical aggregate of weather over thirty-year periods, per WMO convention) should not be conflated with weather itself. The distinction, while elementary, is routinely overlooked in public discourse, leading to categorical errors that undermine productive discussion of atmospheric science.
